strengths: Comprehensive framework addressing real gap: unified VRP environment handling 48 variants is well-designed and practical. Mixed Batch Training (MBT) is well-motivated with convincing empirical validation (Figures 9-11) showing improved stability and convergence across variants.

Efficient Adapter Layers (EAL) elegantly solves catastrophic forgetting in few-shot learning via zero-padding, with Table 2 demonstrating complete failure of standard AL (223% gap at step 0) vs. maintained zero-shot performance with EAL.

Extensive experimental evaluation: 48 VRP variants (3× prior work), thorough ablations (Figures 5, D.3-D.7), out-of-distribution generalization tests (Tables 6-8), and CVRPLIB large-scale evaluation. Global Attribute Embeddings analysis via t-SNE (Figure 13) effectively demonstrates superior variant discrimination.

Strong reproducibility: comprehensive hyperparameter specification (Table 4), detailed data generation procedures (Appendix A.1), promised code release, and clear environment documentation enable reproduction and follow-up work.

Global Attribute Embeddings make interpretable contribution to model representation, with t-SNE analysis showing ROUTEFINDER creates well-defined, tightly grouped clusters compared to baselines, particularly improving time window variant separation (Figure 13).
weaknesses: Confounded experimental setup significantly undermines claims: authors train on 'all available variants' simultaneously while prior work (MTPOMO, MVMoE) trained on single attributes separately. This fundamental difference makes attribution of improvements unclear—performance gain may stem from more diverse training data rather than proposed methods. Direct comparison with identical setup essential but not provided.

Modest performance improvements with limited practical significance: RF-TE vs. MVMoE often differ by only 1-2% in optimality gaps (Table 1, e.g., CVRP n=100: 1.505% vs. 1.694%). Still 2-4% worse than HGS-PyVRP across variants, raising questions about when practitioners should adopt this approach over traditional heuristics. No inference time analysis provided.

Limited novelty in individual components: Transformer improvements (RMS norm, pre-norm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention) are straightforward applications from foundation models in other domains. Reward normalization uses standard techniques (mean/exponential smoothing). Attribute composition extends Liu et al. (2024a) directly. MBT and EAL are main novel contributions but individually modest.

Inadequate scalability analysis: experiments limited to n≤100 in main results. CVRPLIB tests don't employ finetuning (Appendix D.2). Training requires 9-24 hours on A100 GPUs; computational cost never justified or compared to alternatives. Inference time unknown. Whether approach scales to practical problem sizes (n=500+) remains unclear.

EAL improvements modest when properly contextualized: 20% relative improvement over AL (Table 2) but only ~7-19% absolute gain vs. training from scratch (~20% gap with EAL vs. ~23% from scratch). Tested only on relatively minor attribute variations (MD, mixed backhaul); true generalization to fundamentally new constraints undemonstrated.

Missing statistical rigor: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or reported random seed counts. Single test set per variant. Variance in results unknown, making it difficult to assess whether differences are meaningful or within noise.

Inadequate analysis of fitness for purpose: No systematic investigation of when/why ROUTEFINDER is preferable to traditional methods. Foundation model framing is aspirational—this is more accurately a multi-task neural VRP solver. Limited discussion of speed-quality tradeoffs or problem size limitations.

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation on 48 VRP variants (3× prior work) with rigorous ablation studies demonstrating clear contribution of each component

Novel Efficient Adapter Layers (EAL) with zero-padding initialization provides elegant solution for few-shot fine-tuning while maintaining zero-shot performance (Table 2, 20% relative improvement over standard adapters)
Mixed Batch Training effectively addresses training instability for multi-variant learning; Appendix D.5 provides strong empirical validation across variants and imbalanced distributions
Extensive experimental validation including out-of-distribution generalization (Appendix D.1), real-world CVRPLIB evaluation (Appendix D.2), and rich supplementary analyses (t-SNE, encoder ablations)
Well-engineered unified VRP environment supporting 48 variants through modular attribute composition; clear presentation with reproducible implementation details and public code
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core attribute composition framework is from Liu et al. (2024a), and architectural components (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, FlashAttention) are standard modern techniques; contribution is primarily engineering integration
Overstated claims: abstract states '>10% improvement across all variants' but Table 1 shows 1-2% improvements over neural baselines; misleading phrasing reduces credibility

Modest improvements over baselines (1-2% on average) and substantial gap with traditional solvers (e.g., CVRP ROUTEFINDER 1.27% vs HGS optimal); practical applicability limited when traditional methods remain significantly better
Limited scope restricted to VRP domain; does not generalize to other combinatorial optimization problems, reducing the foundation model's ambition despite authors' stated design choice for efficiency

Technical justifications incomplete: why global attribute embeddings outperform alternatives lacks rigorous analysis beyond t-SNE visualization; edge cases in per-variant reward normalization not discussed; no comparison with other parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (LoRA, etc.)
